title: A Provable Oracle-Free Quantum Algorithm for Nonlinear Dynamics on Hybrid Oscillator-Qubit Processors
authors: Kausthubh Chandramouli, Yan Li, Yuan Liu
abstract: We develop a hybrid qubit--qumode algorithm for nonlinear ordinary differential equations of the form $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ with drift of polynomial degree~$L$. Following the Fokker--Planck route of Tennie and Magri, the algorithm propagates the state density and returns the deterministic trajectory as the peak of that density in the small-noise limit. The discretised generator is carried into a parametrised family of Schrödinger equations by the warped-phase transformation of Jin, Liu, and Yu, and the Fourier-mode parameter of that family is placed on a single continuous-variable qumode. Our central structural result is that the Hermitian parts $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ of the discretised generator admit a bipartite Pauli decomposition that sorts the non-zero Pauli strings into $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ mutually commuting families and factorises each family into a diagonal of degree at most $L$ tensored with a fixed rank-two bond operator. The factorisation renders each family exponential an exact product of $\mathcal{O}(n^{L})$ monomial-controlled momentum displacements, with no intra-family Trotter error. On a $d$-dimensional grid of $N=2^{n}$ points per axis the circuit costs $\mathcal{O}(d^{L+1}n^{L+2})$ gates per Trotter step. No sparse-access oracle and no block encoding is invoked: every gate is fixed in closed form by the polynomial coefficients of the drift. We also prove a bound on the numerical abscissa $λ_{\max}(H_{1})$ that fixes the recovery domain of the warped-phase transform and the post-selection cost. A classical simulation on two nonlinear benchmarks confirms the structural theorems, the shifted recovery, and the accuracy-per-resource advantage of the continuous-variable coupling over a discretised mode register.
summary: The paper presents a novel, provably oracle-free quantum algorithm to simulate nonlinear dynamics by linearizing the evolution in the state density using the Fokker–Planck equation. It achieves this by mapping the resulting non-unitary evolution onto a unitary Schrödinger form realized on a hybrid qubit-qumode processor. The core contribution is deriving structural theorems that guarantee an efficient, product-form decomposition of the required quantum gates.
main_problem: Developing a provable, oracle-free quantum algorithm to simulate nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) of the form $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ by propagating the state density.
main_result: The authors establish structural theorems showing that the discretized generator admits a bipartite Pauli decomposition into $O(\log N)$ commuting families, allowing for an exact product representation of the evolution operator with no intra-family Trotter error.
method: The approach uses the Fokker–Planck route to linearize the dynamics in the state density $\rho$, followed by mapping the non-unitary evolution to a parameterized family of unitary Schrödinger equations via the warped-phase transformation. The continuous variable aspect is realized using a qumode coupled to the qubit register.
model_or_system: The system models nonlinear ODEs ($\dot{x} = f(x)$) whose evolution is tracked by propagating the state density $\rho$ governed by a linear transport-diffusion PDE. This PDE is discretized and then mapped onto a quantum Hamiltonian structure involving qubit registers and continuous-variable qumodes.
key_observables: The recovered Probability Density Function ($\rho(x, T)$), the numerical abscissa $\lambda_{\max}(H_1)$, and the gate cost complexity $O(d^{L+1}n^{L+2})$ per Trotter step.
important_parameters: Polynomial drift degree $L$, grid size parameters ($N=2^n$ points on a $d$-dimensional grid), and the time evolution parameter $T$.
main_assumptions: The algorithm is claimed to be oracle-free, meaning gate costs depend only on polynomial coefficients. The analysis relies on structural theorems regarding Pauli decompositions and assumes the validity of the warped-phase transformation.
figures_summary: Figure 5 compares different simulation checks: independent SDE verification, peak tracking, recovered PDF vs. reference, end-to-end error evolution, and a comparison of actual versus theoretically bounded Pauli structures for the logistic law benchmark.
paper_structure: The paper develops structural theorems regarding the Pauli decomposition of the discretized generator ($H_1$ and $H_2$), proves that these terms factorize into monomial displacements, and then applies this framework to simulate nonlinear dynamics using a hybrid qubit-qumode architecture. Comparisons are made against other simulation techniques.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly structured and resource-analyzed quantum algorithm for simulating complex non-equilibrium classical physics problems (nonlinear ODEs) by transforming them into an efficient, hardware-implementable Hamiltonian simulation problem on hybrid processors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Fokker–Planck linearisation ( ˙x = x−x3). (a) An independent Monte-Carlo integration of the stochastic differential equation matches eAT ρ0. (b) The density peak, located by parabolic sub-cell interpolation, follows the deterministic trajectory onto the attractor to within 0.039 in x.

Fig. 2. Pauli structure of H1, H2 (L = 3). (a) Per-family term counts against the original and tightened bounds. (b) The F2 subgroup rank of every family is at most n. (c) The total term count scales as Θ(2n), driven by the suffix multiplicities rather than the degree.

Fig. 3. A discretised (qubit-register) LCU approaching the continuous-variable qumode limit. Each curve fixes the register range ηmax and refines its resolution; the error plateaus at a truncation floor set by ηmax. The qumode realises the joint limit ηmax →∞, ∆η →0 with no register.
Fig. 4. End-to-end validation ( ˙x = x −x3). (a) The recovered density matches the reference eAT ρ0. (b) The relative interior error stays below 10−3 as a function of the simulation time t.

Fig. 5. Logistic benchmark ˙x = r x(1 −x) (L = 2): Fokker–Planck linearisation (top left), end-to-end accuracy (top right), Pauli structure (bottom left), and the continuous-variable versus discretised comparison (bottom right). Compare Figures 1 to 4.
